title: the masks come off
hook: the year ends the way it began, with dice, and then the five servants of Virata's court take the royal seats
carry: acharya devo bhava: the teacher's trust is sacred

segments.voice: Yesterday: a frightened prince ran, a dance teacher ran after him, and at the shami tree outside Virata's city Brihannala told the truth. Your line was Parthasarathy: God holds the reins when fear comes.
screen: `A PRINCE RUNS, A TEACHER FOLLOWS.` · `I AM ARJUNA.`

segments.voice: A conch sounds across the field, and the Kuru warriors know that sound. Arjuna is back. He fights the whole raiding army with Uttara at the reins, and in the end uses a weapon that makes the Kuru warriors fall into a stupor. He sends Uttara among them to take their fine upper cloths, for the princesses' dolls, as promised. The cattle go home. So does a prince who ran away that morning. On this last day of the Virata story, the masks come off.
screen: `A CONCH THE KURUS KNOW.` → `CLOTHS FOR THE DOLLS.` → `THE LAST DAY OF THE MASKS.`

segments.voice: Back at the palace, King Virata is overjoyed. My son has beaten the Kurus! He sits down to dice with Kanka and keeps praising Uttara. Kanka says quietly: with Brihannala driving, how could he lose? Virata, angry, throws the dice in Kanka's face. Blood runs from Yudhishthira's nose, and Sairandhri catches the drops in a vessel before they reach the floor. Brihannala is kept outside, because Arjuna has sworn that whoever draws his brother's blood outside battle will not live. The year began with dice, and it ends with dice, and the hidden king bleeding, still silent. Then the brothers walk in wearing royal clothes, take the royal seats, and Arjuna tells Virata who they are. The king offers his daughter, Princess Uttara, to Arjuna. And Arjuna says no. I was her teacher, he says, and she trusted me as a daughter trusts a father. Let her marry my son, Abhimanyu. Here's the teaching. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, a teacher sends students out into life with these words: let your mother be a god to you, your father, your teacher, your guest. Acharya devo bhava: treat the teacher as divine. It's why Hindu students touch a teacher's feet, and why Guru Purnima is a day to honor teachers. Many teachers read Arjuna's answer as the other side of it: a teacher guards that trust. Today, think of the coaches, tutors and mentors who've held yours. In Hindu teaching, that bond is sacred.
screen: `VIRATA'S DICE STRIKE KANKA` · `THE MASKS COME OFF` · `A TEACHER, NOT A HUSBAND` · then, large: `ACHARYA DEVO BHAVA`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a teacher who mattered to you: at school, at a temple, a coach, a grandparent who taught you a prayer. Many Hindus bow to a teacher, or touch their feet, to say what words can't. Sit tall, bring your palms together at your heart, and breathing in, see their face; breathing out, give your thanks. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer.
Virata. The king who struck his own dice partner, and learned soon after that he had been hosting the Pandavas all year.
Your line: acharya devo bhava: the teacher's trust is sacred. The masks are set down. That's the Virata story, done.

howItsDone: The Virata book closes with the Pandavas revealed and the marriage of Princess Uttara to Abhimanyu, and retellings pause on Arjuna's refusal to marry the student he taught.

chat.meaning: The Upanishad says treat the teacher as divine: acharya devo bhava. Arjuna refused to marry the student who trusted him like a father, because that trust is sacred.

Abhimanyu.meaning: Arjuna's son, who marries Princess Uttara

Uttara.meaning: the name of both King Virata's son and his daughter

Kanka.meaning: Yudhishthira's disguise: a Brahmin who plays dice with the king

Sairandhri.meaning: Draupadi's disguise: a maid who dresses the queen's hair

Brihannala.meaning: Arjuna's disguise: a dance teacher for the palace women

acharya.meaning: a teacher; in 'acharya devo bhava', the teacher honored as divine

recall: a princess sent out to choose a husband

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Virata Parva (Go-harana and Vaivahika), Arjuna's battle with the Kurus, the dice thrown at Kanka, the Pandavas revealed, and the marriage of Uttara and Abhimanyu
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11: the teacher's parting instruction (matri devo bhava, pitri devo bhava, acharya devo bhava, atithi devo bhava)

notes: Audit: first teach head ('Arjuna takes the cloths') named a hook beat the teach never covers; replaced with 'Virata praises his son'. Match pair corrected: in the hook Uttara, not Arjuna, gathers the cloths. Word line 'that evening' cut: the Pandavas reveal themselves days after the dice blow, not the same evening.

All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: the stupefying (sammohana) weapon; Uttara taking the upper garments of the warriors (Ganguli notes Bhishma as an exception); Virata striking Kanka with the dice; Sairandhri catching the blood in a vessel; Brihannala kept outside because of Arjuna's vow.
Confirm that the reveal comes when the Pandavas take the royal seats, and Arjuna's reason for refusing Uttara (he taught her, she trusted him as a father).
The span of Arjuna's teaching is left vague under the claims rule.
